To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effects of hypocaloric feeding on insulin levels and insulin resistance in obese women are related to the body fat distribution.
the effects of a weight-loss program on insulin resistance are greater in women with central-type than with peripheral-type obesity.

the effects of weight loss on body weight, body mass index, body fat and body fat distribution, as well as on insulin and C peptide, are different in women with central-type or peripheral-type obesity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interrelationships between body fat distribution, weight loss and insulin levels in women with central or peripheral type obesity.
the relationship between body weight and fat distribution, on the one hand, and insulin resistance, on the other.
the interrelationships between obesity, body fat distribution, and insulin resistance, and the effect of hypocaloric feeding on these parameters.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the CTO subjects are characterized by higher insulinemia and peripheral insulin resistance which improve during hypocaloric diet probably due to the effect of weight loss combined with the change in body distribution.

the CTO women, who are characterized by an increased risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease, are more prone than the PTO ones to lose weight and body fat, and that this is associated with a significant improvement in their insulin sensitivity.
weight loss in obese women, in addition to its beneficial effect on insulin levels, is also accompanied by a change in body fat redistribution, with a greater effect in women with central obesity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

weight loss and change in body fat patterning in CTO women are accompanied by a reduction of insulin resistance, while weight loss alone in PTO women is not sufficient for a significant improvement of insulin resistance.
weight loss in women with central-type of obesity is accompanied by a greater reduction in fasting and stimulated insulin levels, probably due to a greater reduction in the amount of abdominal fat.
weight loss and the consequent reduction of the WHR are important factors in reducing insulinemia and improving insulin sensitivity in women with central-type, but not peripheral-type obesity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
weight loss is associated with an improvement in insulin resistance and insulin secretion in both groups, but the effect is greater and more consistent in CTO than PTO women.
the body fat distribution is an important determinant of the metabolic effects of obesity.
weight loss and change in body fat patterning may have a role in improving peripheral insulin resistance in obese women with CTO.
